nodes.description: Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used off-label for attack prevention for more than 40 years. About half of patients respond, the response depends on genotype, and some patients with SCN4A variants worsen. It has not been tested in a large randomized trial. How it works is not settled: the systemic acidosis it produces reduces potassium entry into muscle, it opens calcium-activated potassium channels in a rat model by a route that does not depend on carbonic anhydrase inhibition, and it lowers muscle sodium overload in patients with permanent weakness. Long-term use carries a risk of kidney stones, so blood counts, electrolytes and renal ultrasound are monitored.

nodes.description: Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter. In knock-in mouse models of both the sodium-channel and the calcium-channel form of the disease it prevented low-potassium weakness and restored force during an established attack, and it outperformed acetazolamide. The one human trial, a nine-participant crossover study of a single 2 mg dose given at the onset of an exercise-induced focal attack in the hand, did not meet its primary outcome. Bumetanide is not an established treatment for this disease.

nodes.description: Dichlorphenamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and the only drug approved in the United States for primary hypokalemic periodic paralysis. Two sets of randomized, placebo-controlled trials showed fewer attacks in hypokalemic periodic paralysis, and benefit was maintained over a one-year open-label extension. The trials found no effect on muscle strength or muscle mass. Paresthesia and cognitive side effects are common and are usually managed by lowering the dose. Its mechanism is presumed to be that of the class; unlike acetazolamide it is only a weak opener of the muscle BK channel.

nodes.description: The resting potential of a muscle fiber is held by inward-rectifier potassium (Kir) channels, whose outward conductance falls as extracellular potassium falls. In a normal fiber this matters only at very low potassium. In a fiber carrying a gating-pore leak, the remaining potassium conductance can no longer balance the inward leak at potassium concentrations reached during an attack. Potassium salts restore this conductance, and potassium-channel openers (Kv7, KATP or BK) substitute for it. Kir2.1, encoded by KCNJ2, is an inward-rectifier channel of skeletal muscle; KCNJ2 is the Andersen-Tawil syndrome gene and is not a cause of this disease, so it is named here in prose and not bound as one of the entry's genes.

nodes.description: The sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter NKCC1 is the main route of chloride entry into muscle fibers. A higher myoplasmic chloride concentration moves the chloride equilibrium potential in the depolarizing direction and favors the depolarized state of a leaky fiber. Hyperosmolality stimulates the transporter, and chloride also accumulates during the acidosis of sustained exercise. This is a permissive step in the disease, not a defect of the transporter.

Oral potassium chloride is the first-line treatment of an acute attack and can be self-administered at home for moderate attacks. Immediate-release preparations are used; slow-release formulations are usually avoided for acute management. Serum potassium and ECG are monitored where possible, because total body potassium is not depleted and potassium can overshoot as the attack resolves.

nodes.description: The resting potential of an affected fiber is bistable. Instead of hyperpolarizing when extracellular potassium falls, the fiber shifts to a second stable potential near -60 mV. A fraction of fibers sits in this depolarized state even at normal potassium.

animal_models.description: Low-potassium challenge depolarizes the resting potential and abolishes excitability.
animal_models.name: CaV1.1-R528H knock-in mouse

animal_models.description: Insulin induces fiber depolarization and paralysis in potassium-depleted rats.
animal_models.genotype: Wild type, fed a potassium-deficient diet
animal_models.name: Potassium-deficient-diet rat

evidence.reference_title: K+-dependent paradoxical membrane depolarization and Na+ overload, major and reversible contributors to weakness by ion channel leaks.
evidence.snippet: Of myofibers from 7 HypoPP patients, up to 25% were in P2 at a ... of 4 mM, in accordance with their permanent weakness, and up to 99% were in P2 at a ... of 1.5 mM, in accordance with their paralytic attacks.

evidence.reference_title: A calcium channel mutant mouse model of hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: The Ca(V)1.1 R528H mice had a HypoPP phenotype for which low K+ challenge produced a paradoxical depolarization of the resting potential, loss of muscle excitability, and weakness.

nodes.description: Anesthesia and surgery can precipitate attacks. Precautions are strict control of serum potassium, avoidance of large glucose and salt loads, maintenance of body temperature and acid-base balance, and careful use of neuromuscular blocking agents with monitoring of neuromuscular function. A family with the CACNA1S R528H variant has been reported in which one member died of an anesthetic complication resembling malignant hyperthermia.

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Patients with HypoPP are at increased risk for pre‐ or postanesthetic weakness.

evidence.reference_title: Severe prognosis in a large family with hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: in this family three male patients died young, one of them from anesthetic complications resembling malignant hyperthermia.

nodes.description: Some individuals develop fixed, progressive weakness between attacks, often involving proximal lower-limb muscles and reflecting progressive myopathy.

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: A variable myopathy develops in many affected individuals and may result in a progressive muscle weakness predominantly in proximal muscle groups of the lower limbs.

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis: a 3-year follow-up study.
evidence.snippet: The study demonstrates that HypoPP can be a progressive myopathy in both patients with and without attacks of paralysis.

nodes.description: There is no treatment that reverses the fixed myopathy. Physiotherapy is used to maintain strength and motor skills. A trial of supervised strength exercise in hypokalemic and hyperkalemic periodic paralysis is recruiting.

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: There is no known curative treatment for hypoPP-related myopathy; physiotherapy may help to maintain strength and motor skills.

nodes.description: Pinacidil is an opener of ATP-sensitive potassium channels. A small controlled study reported improved muscle strength in two of four participants, but hypotension limits the dose that can be given, and in mouse muscle it is about ten times less potent than retigabine. It is not used in practice.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment for periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: pinacidil, a potassium channel opener, also improved muscle strength in 2/4 participants with HypoPP in a third study.

evidence.reference_title: Retigabine suppresses loss of force in mouse models of hypokalaemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: in clinical practice intolerable hypotension occurred before a meaningful improvement of muscle function was obtained.

nodes.description: Rats made hypokalemic by diet become paralyzed and their fibers depolarize after insulin. This is the model in which acetazolamide and other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors were found to open the muscle calcium-activated potassium channel. The rats carry no channel variant.

High-carbohydrate meals, high salt intake, alcohol, stress, and rest after strenuous exercise can precipitate attacks in genetically susceptible skeletal muscle by promoting potassium shifts or sarcolemmal inexcitability.

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Positive triggers (high carbohydrate rich meal, rest after exercise, stress)

evidence.reference_title: Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis: a case induced by concurrent hyperthyroidism.
evidence.snippet: A 40-year-old African American man presented with profound muscle weakness after consuming a high-salt meal.

nodes.description: A subset of affected individuals develop fixed or progressive myopathy with permanent weakness and increasing fatty replacement of skeletal muscle, which can progress even in people without frequent paralytic attacks. In the CaV1.1-R528H mouse the myopathy is vacuolar, with dilated transverse tubules and disrupted triad junctions.

animal_models.description: The mice develop a vacuolar myopathy with mild permanent weakness.
animal_models.name: CaV1.1-R528H knock-in mouse

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis: a 3-year follow-up study.
evidence.snippet: Muscle strength declined in 11 patients during follow-up.

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis: a 3-year follow-up study.
evidence.snippet: Fat replacement of muscles increased in 27 patients during follow-up.

evidence.reference_title: A calcium channel mutant mouse model of hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: A vacuolar myopathy with dilated transverse tubules and disruption of the triad junctions impaired Ca2+ release and likely contributed to the mild permanent weakness.

nodes.description: Severe attacks can rarely include respiratory muscle weakness or paralysis, particularly in complex presentations with profound hypokalemia or secondary triggers.

evidence.reference_title: Case report: SCN4A p.R1135H gene variant in combination with thyrotoxicosis causing hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: It is a rare case of SCN4A p.R1135H gene variant combined with hyperthyroidism resulting in HPP with respiratory muscle paralysis

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis
evidence.snippet: HP:0002747 | Respiratory insufficiency due to muscle weakness | Occasional (29-5%)

nodes.description: Weakness that comes on during rest after vigorous exercise is the most common trigger. In mouse models, recovery from a period of acidosis, as after exercise, produces a loss of force that depends on chloride entry into the fiber.

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: The major triggering factors are cessation of effort following strenuous exercise and carbohydrate-rich evening meals.

nodes.description: Retigabine (ezogabine) is an opener of Kv7 (KCNQ) voltage-gated potassium channels. In knock-in mouse models of both genetic forms it prevented the loss of force produced by a low-potassium challenge and reversed an established loss of force, at low micromolar concentrations. It has not been tested in patients with this disease, and it is no longer distributed as an antiseizure drug.

evidence.reference_title: Retigabine suppresses loss of force in mouse models of hypokalaemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Application of retigabine also reversed the loss of force (rescue) for HypoPP muscle maintained in 2 mM K+.

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy of Retigabine in Treating Weakness in a Mouse Model of Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Retigabine significantly reduced loss of force at both 4.75 and 1.0 mM K+ (p = 0.047 and p = 0.007, respectively).

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy of a K(+) Channel Agonist, XEN1101, For Preserving Contractility in Mouse Models of Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: was approved for adjuvant therapy in partial seizures ... but then removed from distribution with a black‐box warning of pigmentary changes in skin and retina

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: HypoPP is associated with mutations in calcium channel (CACNA1S; 60% of kindreds) and sodium channel (SCN4A; 20% of kindreds) genes.

evidence.reference_title: Case report: SCN4A p.R1135H gene variant in combination with thyrotoxicosis causing hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: genetic testing indicated a missense variant, NM_000334.4 (SCN4A):c.3404G>A (p.R1135H).

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: the identification of a heterozygous pathogenic variant in CACNA1S or SCN4A

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Low serum potassium is not due to low total body potassium but rather shifts of potassium from the blood compartment into the intracellular muscle compartment.

meta.presence: Decreased during attacks, normal between attacks

readouts.interpretation: A fall in serum potassium during an attack reads out the shift of potassium into muscle. It is also what is monitored during potassium replacement, because potassium can overshoot as the shift reverses.

nodes.description: A daily slow-release potassium salt is used as chronic preventive therapy, alongside trigger avoidance and before a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor is added. There are no randomized trials to guide the dose.

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Although no randomized controlled studies are available to inform dosing, a daily slow‐release potassium salt formulation may be considered the standard of care for chronic therapy.

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: This may be achieved by avoidance of triggering factors, adherence to a diet low in sodium and carbohydrate and rich in potassium, and with the use of oral potassium supplementation.

nodes.description: In a depolarized fiber the voltage-gated sodium channels are inactivated, action potentials fail, and the fiber cannot be recruited for contraction.
nodes.id: Sodium-Channel Inactivation and Loss of Fiber Excitability

animal_models.description: Low-potassium challenge produces transient loss of excitability and weakness.
animal_models.genotype: Scn4a p.R669H knock-in (ortholog of human SCN4A R669H), homozygous
animal_models.name: NaV1.4-R669H knock-in mouse

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: In all forms of PP, ictal paresis is caused by depolarization of the muscle sarcolemma, which in turn causes sodium channel inactivation and reduced fiber excitability.

evidence.reference_title: A sodium channel knockin mutant (NaV1.4-R669H) mouse model of hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Homozygous R669H mice had a robust HypoPP phenotype, with transient loss of muscle excitability and weakness in low-K+ challenge, insensitivity to high-K+ challenge, dominant inheritance, and absence of myotonia.

nodes.description: Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and potassium-sparing diuretic used as a chronic preventive option when carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are not tolerated or not effective. It reduces renal potassium loss. The recommendation rests on expert opinion; no controlled trial has tested it in this disease. It may be combined with potassium supplements, with regular monitoring of serum potassium.

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: If carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are not tolerated or not effective after prolonged use, alternatives include potassium-sparing diuretics such as triamterene, spironolactone, or eplerenone.

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Recommended doses are triamterene 50–150 mg/day, spironolactone 25–100 mg/day or eplerenone 50–100 mg daily.

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Spironolactone may be poorly tolerated because of androgenic side effects, and epleronone may be substituted because it causes fewer hormonal issues.

evidence.reference_title: Practical aspects in the management of hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Chronically, acetazolamide, dichlorphenamide, or potassium-sparing diuretics decrease attack frequency and severity

nodes.description: Topiramate is an antiseizure drug with carbonic anhydrase inhibitory activity. A report of 11-year-old twins described less severe attacks after it was started. The evidence is limited to case reports.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment of hypokalemic periodic paralysis with topiramate.
evidence.snippet: The patients experienced a decrease in the severity of their attacks upon initiation of treatment.

nodes.description: Triamterene is a potassium-sparing diuretic listed with spironolactone and eplerenone as a chronic preventive alternative. Its use rests on expert opinion.

evidence.reference_title: Review of the Diagnosis and Treatment of Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Recommended doses are triamterene 50–150 mg/day, spironolactone 25–100 mg/day or eplerenone 50–100 mg daily.

evidence.reference_title: Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis.
evidence.snippet: If carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are not tolerated or not effective after prolonged use, alternatives include potassium-sparing diuretics such as triamterene, spironolactone, or eplerenone.

nodes.description: Dietary and behavioral counseling targets common triggers such as high-carbohydrate meals, high salt intake, alcohol, stress, and rest after strenuous exercise. Patients with CACNA1S-related disease report that regular meals with controlled portions of complex carbohydrate, regular mild to moderate exercise with warm-up and cool-down, and avoiding inactivity make them less vulnerable, and that triggers add up.

evidence.reference_title: Practical aspects in the management of hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence.snippet: Avoidance of or potassium prophylaxis for common triggers, such as rest after exercise, high carbohydrate meals, and sodium, can prevent attacks.

evidence.reference_title: A novel CACNA1S gene variant in a child with hypokalemic periodic paralysis: a case report and literature review.
evidence.snippet: The attacks of the patient are prevented by lifestyle changes and nutritional counseling.

evidence.reference_title: Exploring self-management of diet and physical activity in CACNA1S-related hypokalemic periodic paralysis: A qualitative interview study.
evidence.snippet: The participants experienced that regular meals with controlled portions of complex carbohydrates, limited intake of simple carbohydrates, engaging in regular mild to moderate exercise combined with warm-up and cool-down, and avoiding physical inactivity made them less vulnerable to attacks of muscle weakness and paralysis.
